title: Unfair Security Deposit Deductions: A Renter's Guide
summary: Understand security deposit deductions, learn your rights, and discover how to protect your finances as a tenant. Get informed and safeguard your deposit today!
body_text: Security deposits: that chunk of change you hand over at the start of a lease, hoping to see it again intact when you move out. But between normal wear and tear, potential damages, and sometimes overzealous landlords, getting your full deposit back can feel like an uphill battle. This guide is your comprehensive resource for understanding everything about security deposit deductions. We'll cover what's considered a legitimate deduction, how to document your rental's condition, and what steps to take if you believe you've been unfairly charged. Consider this your go-to guide for protecting your finances and your rights as a renter. Key Takeaways Create a thorough record of your rental's condition: Document everything from day one. Detailed photos, videos, and a written inventory from your move-in and move-out inspections are crucial for protecting yourself against unwarranted charges. Know your state's security deposit laws: Research your local regulations regarding permissible deductions, maximum deposit amounts, and required return timeframes. This knowledge empowers you to advocate for your rights. Maintain open communication with your landlord: Address any maintenance issues and potential deduction concerns promptly and respectfully. Proactive communication can often resolve disagreements and prevent disputes. What Are Security Deposit Deductions? Security deposit deductions are amounts withheld from your security deposit by your landlord. Landlords can make these deductions to cover unpaid rent and damage to the rental unit, excluding normal wear and tear. Think of your security deposit as a financial safeguard for the landlord, covering potential costs incurred during your tenancy. It's important to understand what constitutes a legitimate deduction to protect yourself from unfair charges. Review state laws regarding security deposits. Most states require landlords to provide tenants with an itemized list of each deduction and its associated cost, promoting transparency and allowing you to review the charges. What Is Normal Wear and Tear? Normal wear and tear refers to the unavoidable deterioration of a property from everyday use. It's the natural consequence of living in a space, and landlords shouldn't deduct from your security deposit for these minor issues. Think small scuffs on the walls , slightly faded paint, or a loose door handle from repeated use—these are considered normal wear and tear. Learn more about common security deposit deductions. Understanding the difference between normal wear and tear and actual damage is crucial for both renters and landlords. Common & Legitimate Deductions While normal wear and tear is expected, several common and legitimate reasons exist for a landlord to deduct from your security deposit. Unpaid rent is a straightforward example. If you owe rent at the end of your lease, your landlord can deduct this amount from your deposit. Damages beyond normal wear and tear are another common reason. This could include pet damage, broken appliances (beyond normal use), or significant damage to walls or flooring. Excessive cleaning fees are also permissible if the property is left unreasonably dirty upon your departure. Find a detailed list of potential deductions here. Familiarizing yourself with these common deductions can help you avoid surprises and prepare for potential costs when moving out. This resource offers further clarification on legitimate deductions. When Deductions Become Excessive Sometimes, security deposit deductions cross the line from reasonable to excessive. Knowing how to spot these situations and understanding your options is key to protecting your finances. Identify Unreasonable Charges Landlords can deduct from your security deposit for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, and excessive cleaning costs. It’s important to understand what constitutes “normal wear and tear” versus actual damage. For example, small nail holes from hanging pictures are generally considered normal wear and tear, while a large hole in the wall from a doorknob isn't. Similarly, worn carpet from regular use over time is considered normal, but a large stain from a spilled drink is likely damage. Your landlord must provide you with an itemized statement explaining each deduction, giving you a chance to discuss the charges before they're finalized. This transparency is crucial, allowing you to understand the basis of each charge and contest any that seem unreasonable. If your landlord claims you owe more than the initial deposit amount, make sure you understand your state's laws regarding this, as it may not be permissible. Remember, documentation is key. Keep records of your communication with your landlord, including any agreements made about repairs. How Overcharging Impacts Tenants Excessive deductions can significantly impact a renter's finances, especially when moving between apartments. Unexpectedly high charges can derail budgeting and make it difficult to afford moving expenses or a new security deposit. Beyond the immediate financial strain, unfair deductions can also create stress and anxiety. Disputing these charges can be time-consuming and emotionally draining. Accurate documentation of your interactions with your landlord is vital. This documentation can include photographs of the property , repair requests, and other supporting evidence that demonstrates the condition of the rental unit at the time of move-out. Maintaining detailed records of all interactions with your landlord, including dates, times, and descriptions of conversations, is crucial in disputing excessive charges . If you believe your landlord is making unreasonable deductions, knowing your rights and how to document your case is the first step toward getting your money back. Know Your Rights as a Tenant Understanding your rights as a renter is crucial, especially when it comes to security deposits. Landlords can't simply keep your deposit without a valid reason. Knowing the laws in your state helps you avoid unnecessary financial strain and protects you from unfair practices. State Laws Protecting You Security deposit laws protect renters from excessive charges and ensure the timely return of their money. These laws vary by state, covering key areas like the maximum deposit amount a landlord can request, the timeframe for returning the deposit, and acceptable reasons for deductions. For example, many states limit the security deposit to one or two months' rent. They also outline specific reasons a landlord can deduct from the deposit, such as unpaid rent or damages beyond normal wear and tear. Hemlane's state-by-state guide offers detailed information on your local regulations. Time Limits on Deposit Returns How long does a landlord have to return your security deposit? This depends on your state. While the typical timeframe is two to four weeks after you move out, some states allow longer. Regardless, landlords must return the deposit within a reasonable timeframe. Check iPropertyManagement's overview of state laws to confirm the specific regulations where you live. What Happens With Late Returns? What if your landlord doesn't return your deposit on time? There can be legal consequences. In many jurisdictions, if a landlord fails to return the deposit in full and doesn't provide an itemized list of damages with supporting documentation (like repair costs and receipts), they may be required to return the entire deposit. Nolo's resource offers further information on the potential repercussions landlords face for not complying with these laws. Knowing these details empowers you to advocate for yourself and ensure you receive your deposit back as legally required. Document Your Rental's Condition Protecting your security deposit starts long before you move out. Thorough documentation of your rental's condition is key to avoiding disputes and ensuring a full refund. Think of it as building a solid defense against potential disagreements. Move-In & Move-Out Inspections The move-in inspection is your first chance to document the property's condition. Don't rush this process. Carefully note any existing damage, no matter how small. Attorney Aaron Hall emphasizes the importance of documentation in tenant disputes, stating that it "provides key evidence in establishing a paper trail of events" ( source ). This advice applies from day one. A thorough move-in inspection report, complete with photos and videos, protects you from being held responsible for pre-existing issues. The move-out inspection offers a final opportunity to document the condition after your tenancy. Attend this inspection and document everything jointly with your landlord. Create a Thorough Inventory Go beyond simply noting existing damage. Create a detailed inventory of every item in the rental, including appliances, fixtures, and the condition of walls and floors. Be specific. For example, instead of "stove in good condition," note any scratches, dents, or malfunctions. This inventory acts as a snapshot of the property's condition at the start of your lease, invaluable when comparing the state of the rental at move-out. Document with Photos & Videos Visual documentation is crucial. Use your phone or camera to take clear photos and videos of each room, paying close attention to areas prone to wear and tear. As Brennan Property Management advises, "Take detailed photographs or videos of each room, focusing on areas that may be prone to wear and tear" ( source ). Document minor details like scuffs on the walls or loose cabinet handles. Date and time-stamp your photos and videos if possible, and store them securely. This visual record, combined with your written inventory, provides compelling evidence of the rental's condition at both move-in and move-out. This visual documentation, as highlighted by Sam Law, is crucial supporting evidence in landlord-tenant disputes ( source ). Challenge Unfair Security Deposit Deductions Getting your security deposit back can sometimes feel like pulling teeth. But don't worry, you have options. Here's how to challenge unfair deductions and get what you're rightfully owed. Request an Itemized Statement Your first step is to get a detailed account of why your landlord is withholding any portion of your security deposit. Most states require landlords to provide an itemized list of every deduction, specifying the exact costs. This transparency is key to understanding the basis of the deductions. If your landlord isn't providing this information, refer to your state's landlord-tenant laws (often available online through your state's housing authority website) and remind them of their obligations. This itemized statement is your roadmap to challenging unfair charges. Communicate with Your Landlord Before things escalate, try talking to your landlord. Often, a simple conversation can clear up misunderstandings. Maybe there's a mistake in the statement, or perhaps they can provide further clarification on the charges. Explain your concerns calmly and respectfully, focusing on the specific deductions you believe are unjustified. For example, if you're being charged for "excessive cleaning," ask for specifics. What exactly was excessively dirty, and why does it warrant that cost? Open communication can often resolve disputes and prevent them from becoming bigger problems. Write a Formal Dispute Letter If talking it out doesn't work, put your concerns in writing. A formal dispute letter creates a documented record of your disagreement. In your letter, clearly state which deductions you're disputing and why. Provide evidence to support your claims, such as photos, videos, or receipts for repairs you made. Refer to your lease agreement and any relevant state laws. A template can be helpful for structuring your letter, but make sure to personalize it with your specific situation and details. Keep a copy of the letter for your records and send it via certified mail for proof of delivery. This letter sets the stage for further action if needed. Explore Legal Options If you’ve tried resolving a security deposit dispute directly with your landlord and haven’t gotten anywhere, it’s time to consider other options. Don’t feel discouraged—you have several legal avenues to explore. Knowing your rights and the resources available can help you get your deposit back. Small Claims Court Small claims court offers a way to resolve disputes involving smaller amounts of money, which makes it a good option for many security deposit disagreements. The process is generally less formal than other court proceedings, and you typically don't need a lawyer. However, it's always a good idea to familiarize yourself with your state's specific small claims procedures. If you feel you've taken good care of the property and disagree with the deductions, this can be an effective way to pursue your claim. Just remember to gather all necessary documentation, like your lease agreement, photos, and any communication with your landlord. Mediation & Dispute Resolution Before heading to court, consider mediation. This involves a neutral third party who helps facilitate communication and negotiation between you and your landlord. It’s often less adversarial and more cost-effective than going to court. Many states and cities offer free or low-cost mediation services specifically for landlord-tenant disputes. Check with your local housing authority or renter's rights organization for resources in your area. As with other legal options, having your documentation organized will help you present your case clearly. Seek Legal Assistance If mediation is unsuccessful, or if the disputed amount is substantial, seeking legal counsel from a qualified attorney specializing in landlord-tenant law is a smart move. A lawyer can advise you on the best course of action, help you understand your rights, and represent you in court if necessary. Good documentation is crucial for any legal action. Make sure you’ve compiled all relevant documents, including your lease, correspondence with your landlord, photos, videos, and any other evidence that supports your claim. This will help your lawyer build a strong case. Prevent Future Disputes Dealing with security deposit deductions can be a real headache. Proactively taking steps to avoid disputes is always the smartest move. Here’s how: Understand Your Lease Your lease is your roadmap as a renter. It outlines the terms of your tenancy, including everything about your security deposit. Carefully review this section to understand: Allowed deductions: What can your landlord legally deduct from your security deposit? Common examples include unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, and cleaning costs. Knowing what’s permissible upfront helps you avoid surprises later. Documentation requirements: Does your lease specify any required documentation for move-in/move-out inspections? Understanding these requirements from the start can prevent disagreements down the road. Security deposit limits: Many states have laws capping how much a landlord can charge for a security deposit. Familiarize yourself with your state’s specific security deposit laws to ensure your landlord is following the rules. These laws often cover the maximum deposit amount, the timeline for return, and acceptable deductions. Knowing your lease agreement inside and out empowers you to address any potential issues early on. Maintain Open Communication A positive landlord-tenant relationship hinges on clear communication. Keep the lines of communication open with your landlord throughout your tenancy. This includes: Regular updates: If something breaks or needs repair, notify your landlord promptly. Don’t wait until a small problem becomes a big one. This shows you’re a responsible tenant and helps prevent disputes about repair responsibility. Move-out notice: Provide proper notice according to your lease agreement. This gives your landlord adequate time to prepare for the move-out inspection and avoids misunderstandings. Clarify concerns: If you have any questions or concerns about potential deductions, discuss them with your landlord before you move out. Addressing potential issues proactively can often prevent them from escalating into formal disputes. Open communication is the key to resolving disagreements amicably. Regular Property Maintenance Taking good care of your rental is crucial for preventing disputes over the security deposit. Consider these tips: Routine cleaning: Regularly clean your apartment, including vacuuming, mopping, and wiping down surfaces. This prevents the buildup of dirt and grime that can sometimes be mistaken for damage. Minor repairs: Address minor repairs yourself, if you’re comfortable and your lease allows. For example, tightening a loose doorknob or fixing a dripping faucet can prevent more significant damage later. Always check with your landlord before undertaking any repairs. Document everything: Document the condition of your rental when you move in and when you move out. Take photos and videos of each room, paying close attention to any existing damage. This documentation can be incredibly helpful if a dispute arises. By being proactive and communicative, you can significantly reduce the risk of security deposit deductions and make your move-out process much smoother. Protect Your Deposit from Day One Getting your security deposit back shouldn't feel like a battle. A little proactive planning can make all the difference. Start protecting your deposit the moment you begin your apartment search. Choose a Reputable Landlord Finding a good landlord can save you from deposit drama down the road. Do your research before signing a lease. Look for landlords with positive reviews and a history of treating tenants fairly. Online resources and local tenant forums can be invaluable tools for gathering insights. Understanding your state's security deposit laws is also crucial. These laws dictate things like the maximum deposit amount and the timeframe for its return after you move out. Resources like Hemlane and Landlord Studio offer comprehensive guides to these laws by state, empowering you to understand your rights from the start. Knowing these regulations helps you spot potential red flags early on. The Role of Renters Insurance Renters insurance is your best friend when it comes to protecting your belongings and your deposit. While it primarily covers your personal property against issues like theft, fire, or water damage, it can also provide liability protection. This means if you accidentally damage the property, your renters insurance might cover the costs, preventing deductions from your security deposit. Think of it as a safety net. Beyond financial protection, having renters insurance demonstrates responsibility. It shows you’re taking steps to mitigate potential risks, which can contribute to a positive landlord-tenant relationship. Accurate documentation is key in any dispute, so keeping records of your insurance policy and communication with your landlord is always wise. Resources like this one from attorney Aaron Hall and this guide from Sam Law offer additional tips on documenting landlord-tenant interactions. A little preparation can go a long way. Take Action: Unfairly Withheld Deposit Dealing with an unfairly withheld security deposit is frustrating, but you have options. Taking clear, decisive action is key to getting your money back. Here’s a strategic approach: Gather Evidence Building a strong case requires organization and thoroughness. Collect all relevant documents related to your tenancy: your lease agreement, correspondence with your landlord (emails, texts, letters), rent receipts, and move-in/move-out inspection reports. Photos and videos of the rental unit’s condition are crucial. Thorough documentation creates a clear paper trail, essential if you need to pursue legal action. Solid evidence is paramount ( source ). Accurate records of all interactions with your landlord, including dates, times, and descriptions of conversations, are also helpful ( source ). File a Formal Complaint Once you’ve gathered your evidence, formally address the issue. Most states require landlords to provide an itemized list of each security deposit deduction with the cost ( source ). Request this from your landlord. If deductions seem unreasonable or contradict your documentation, write a formal dispute letter. Clearly outline the disputed charges, referencing your evidence and citing relevant state laws. Keep a copy for your records. Landlords typically have 30 days to return security deposits if all lease terms are met ( source ). If your landlord is unresponsive or doesn't return the deposit within the legal timeframe, you can escalate. In court, the burden of proof is on the landlord ( source ). Leverage Tenant Advocacy Resources You're not alone. Several resources offer support and guidance. Familiarize yourself with your state’s security deposit laws, which often cover maximum deposit amounts, acceptable deductions, and required return timelines ( source ). Local tenant advocacy groups are invaluable, offering advice, resources, and legal referrals ( source ). Contact these organizations for help understanding your rights and navigating the process. Knowledge is power, especially in these situations. Related Articles How Landlord-Tenant Laws Work in Pennsylvania (Full Guide) | Goodcover – fair, modern, cooperative renters insurance. Moving Soon? Use a Rental Inspection Checklist for Tenants | Goodcover – fair, modern, cooperative renters insurance. Frequently Asked Questions about Security Deposits What is "normal wear and tear" versus actual damage? Normal wear and tear refers to the expected deterioration of a property from everyday use, like minor scuffs on walls or slightly faded paint. Actual damage, on the other hand, goes beyond this, encompassing things like significant holes in the wall, burns on the carpet, or broken appliances due to misuse. It's the difference between the unavoidable effects of living in a space and damage caused by negligence or misuse. My landlord is withholding my entire security deposit. What can I do? First, request an itemized statement outlining each deduction and its associated cost. Many states require landlords to provide this. If the deductions seem unreasonable or lack proper documentation, communicate with your landlord to discuss your concerns. If this doesn't resolve the issue, consider writing a formal dispute letter outlining your disagreements and referencing supporting evidence. If necessary, explore legal options like small claims court or mediation. Remember, local tenant advocacy groups can offer valuable support and guidance. How can I document the condition of my rental effectively? Conduct a thorough move-in inspection, noting any existing damage with photos and videos. Create a detailed inventory of every item, including appliances and fixtures. Repeat this process during the move-out inspection. Date and time-stamp your documentation whenever possible. This comprehensive record will be invaluable if disputes arise later. What are my rights regarding security deposit deductions? Your rights vary by state, but generally, landlords can only deduct for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear and tear, and sometimes, excessive cleaning. Many states limit the amount a landlord can charge for a security deposit and regulate the timeframe for its return. Research your state's specific landlord-tenant laws or consult with a local tenant advocacy group to understand your rights fully. How can I prevent security deposit disputes in the future? Choose a reputable landlord with a history of fair treatment. Thoroughly understand your lease agreement, especially the section on security deposits. Maintain open communication with your landlord, addressing any concerns promptly. Document the condition of your rental at move-in and move-out with photos, videos, and a detailed inventory. Consider renters insurance for added protection. Proactive communication and documentation are key to a smooth move-out process.

title: Bishop Street Underwriters Announces Strategic Investment by White Mountains
summary: Strategic Investment to Support and Accelerate Growth NEW YORK, NY, February 26, 2026 – Bishop Street Underwriters (“Bishop Street”), a RedBird Capital Partners portfolio company, today announced that it has completed a strategic structured capital investment of $125 million by White Mountains
body_text: Bishop Street Underwriters Announces Strategic Investment by White Mountains February 26, 2026 at 5:00 PM EST PDF Version Strategic Investment to Support and Accelerate Growth NEW YORK, NY, February 26, 2026 – Bishop Street Underwriters (“Bishop Street”), a RedBird Capital Partners portfolio company, today announced that it has completed a strategic structured capital investment of $125 million by White Mountains Insurance Group, Ltd. (“White Mountains”) (NYSE: WTM). "We are thrilled to welcome White Mountains as a strategic growth partner during a period of unprecedented momentum,” said Chad Levine, Chief Executive Officer of Bishop Street Underwriters. “Bishop Street’s 2025 performance - surpassing $650 million in gross written premium and industry leading organic growth while maintaining a stellar sub-50 percent portfolio loss ratio - validates our commitment to backing elite underwriters, pursuing accretive acquisitions and launching de novo programs. With the addition of White Mountains as a strategic partner, we will look to accelerate our strategy and cement our global footprint in 2026." Chad Weber, President of Bishop Street Underwriters, added "White Mountains brings a formidable history of scaling successful MGAs, a deep-seated knowledge of the MGA landscape and an understanding of the intricacies of our industry. We are excited to welcome their expertise to our boardroom and leverage their capabilities and connectivity to unlock new opportunities for the platform and our operating partners." Liam Caffrey, Chief Executive Officer of White Mountains, said, “Bishop Street is quickly emerging as an industry-leading MGA platform. This is a talented executive team with a strong track record of scaling insurance distribution businesses. We believe Bishop Street is well positioned to capitalize on secular growth tailwinds.” Chris Delehanty, Head of M&A of White Mountains added, “We are pleased to partner with RedBird and a team we’ve known for many years. We look forward to collaborating on opportunities to accelerate the company’s growth and performance.” Mike Zabik, Partner at RedBird Capital Partners, said, “White Mountains is a long-term investor, with deep insurance expertise, an outstanding track record and relevant resources to make them the ideal partner for Bishop Street and RedBird. With an established global footprint and significant opportunities for growth and partnership, this investment and partnership will allow Bishop Street to capitalize on its growth objectives in 2026 and beyond.” About Bishop Street Underwriters Bishop Street Underwriters, a RedBird Capital Partners portfolio company, seeks to partner with Managing General Agents (“MGAs”) as well as niche underwriting teams. Bishop Street aims to combine their best-in-class (re)insurance executive team's vision with RedBird’s strong track record, expertise and network in the financial services sector to build a differentiated platform that is uniquely positioned to capitalize on secular growth tailwinds in the industry. For more information, please go to www.bishopstreetuw.com. About White Mountains White Mountains is a Bermuda-domiciled financial services holding company traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol WTM and on the Bermuda Stock Exchange under the symbol WTM.BH. Additional financial information and other items of interest are available at the Company's web site located at www.whitemountains.com. About RedBird Capital Partners RedBird Capital Partners is a private investment firm that builds high-growth companies and provides strategic capital solutions to founders and entrepreneurs. Founded in 2014 by Gerry Cardinale, RedBird integrates sophisticated private equity investing with a hands-on business building mandate, focusing on two core ecosystems – Sports, Media & Entertainment and Financial Services. The firm currently manages over $14 billion in assets on behalf of a global group of blue chip institutional and family office investors. For more information, please go to www.redbirdcap.com. body_text: Our parent Company, Old Republic International Corporation (NYSE: ORI), announced that its Board of Directors has declared a regular quarterly cash dividend of 31.5 cents per share. title: Mtron Hosts and Sponsors the Orlando Science High School robotics team
summary: Mtron designs and manufactures high-reliability RF filters, oscillators, resonators, frequency control, spectrum control, and integrated microwave solutions for aerospace, defense, space, avionics, communications, and mission-critical applications.
body_text: ORLANDO, Fla., Feb. 24, 2026 – Mtron (NYSE American: MPTI), a leading provider of high-performance radio frequency (“RF”) components and solutions, was pleased to host and sponsor students from the Orlando Science High School robotics team as they prepare to enter the 2026 FIRST® Tech Challenge and the 2026 FIRST® Robotics Competition, the World’s Largest K-12 Robotics Event. Founded in 1989 by inventor Dean Kamen, FIRST (For Inspiration and Recognition of Science and Technology) prepares young people for the future through a suite of welcoming, team-based robotics programs for ages 5-18 (K-12). Starting with a kit of parts, teams of high school students design, program, and build industrial-sized robots to play an action-packed game. They compete on a themed field as part of a three-team alliance in the spirit of Coopertition ®. Guided by adult mentors, each FIRST ® Robotics Competition team creates a team identity, raises funds to meet its goals, and advances appreciation for STEM in its community. About Mtron M-tron Industries, Inc. (NYSE American: MPTI) designs, manufactures, and markets highly engineered, high reliability frequency and spectrum control products and solutions. As an engineering-centric company, Mtron provides close support to its customers throughout our products’ entire life cycle, including product design, prototyping, production, and subsequent product upgrades. Mtron has design and manufacturing facilities in Orlando, Florida, and Yankton, South Dakota, a sales office in Hong Kong, and a manufacturing facility in Noida, India.

NOTES Non-GAAP Financial Measures Non-GAAP financial measures are intended to provide additional information only and do not have any standard meaning prescribed by United States generally accepted accounting principles ("GAAP"). These measures should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for measures of performance prepared in accordance with GAAP. The non-GAAP financial measures cited in this release and listed below are reconciled to their most comparable GAAP measure at the end of this release. (1) Free cash flow is a non-GAAP measure calculated as cash provided by operating activities less capital investment. Cash provided by operating activities for the Greens Creek, Lucky Friday, Keno Hill, and Casa Berardi operations excludes exploration and pre-development investment, as it is a discretionary expenditure and not a component of the mines’ operating performance. Capital investment refers to Additions to properties, plants and equipment from the Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, net of finance leases. (2) Cash cost, after by-product credits, per silver and gold ounce is a non-GAAP measurement, a reconciliation of total cost of sales, can be found at the end of the release. It is an important operating statistic that management utilizes to measure each mine's operating performance. It also allows the benchmarking of performance of each mine versus those of our competitors. As a primary silver mining company, management also uses the statistic on an aggregate basis - aggregating the Greens Creek and Lucky Friday mines to compare performance with that of other silver mining companies. Similarly, the statistic is useful in identifying acquisition and investment opportunities as it provides a common tool for measuring the financial performance of other mines with varying geologic, metallurgical and operating characteristics. In addition, the Company may use it when formulating performance goals and targets under its incentive program. (3) All-in sustaining cost ("AISC"), after by-product credits, is a non-GAAP measurement, a reconciliation of which to total cost of sales, the closest GAAP measurement, can be found in the end of the release. AISC, after by-product credits, includes total cost of sales and other direct production costs, expenses for reclamation at the mine sites and all site sustaining capital costs. AISC, after by-product credits, is calculated net of depreciation, depletion, and amortization and by-product credits. Current GAAP measures used in the mining industry, such as total cost of goods sold, do not capture all the expenditures incurred to discover, develop and sustain silver and gold production. Management believes that AISC is a non-GAAP measure that provides additional information to management, investors and analysts to help (i) in the understanding of the economics of our operations and performance compared to other producers and (ii) in the transparency by better defining the total costs associated with production. Similarly, the statistic is useful in identifying acquisition and investment opportunities as it provides a common tool for measuring the financial performance of other mines with varying geologic, metallurgical and operating characteristics. In addition, the Company may use it when formulating performance goals and targets under its incentive program. (4) Adjusted EBITDA is a non-GAAP measurement, a reconciliation of which to net income, the most comparable GAAP measure, can be found at the end of the release. Adjusted EBITDA is a measure used by management to evaluate the Company's operating performance but should not be considered an alternative to net income, or cash provided by operating activities as those terms are defined by GAAP, and does not necessarily indicate whether cash flows will be sufficient to fund cash needs. In addition, the Company may use it when formulating performance goals and targets under its incentive program. Net debt to adjusted EBITDA is a non-GAAP measurement, a reconciliation of which to debt and net income, the most comparable GAAP measurements, can be found at the end of the release. It is an important measure for management to measure relative indebtedness and the ability to service the debt relative to its peers. It is calculated as total debt outstanding less total cash on hand divided by adjusted EBITDA. Current GAAP measures used in the mining industry, such as cost of goods sold, do not capture all the expenditures incurred to discover, develop and sustain silver and gold production. Cash Cost, After By-product Credits, per Ounce and AISC, After By-product Credits, per Ounce also allow us to benchmark the performance of each of our mines versus those of our competitors. As a silver and gold mining company, we also use these statistics on an aggregate basis - aggregating the Greens Creek and Lucky Friday mines to compare our performance with that of other silver mining companies. Similarly, these statistics are useful in identifying acquisition and investment opportunities as they provide a common tool for measuring the financial performance of other mines with varying geologic, metallurgical and operating characteristics. Cash Cost, Before By-product Credits and AISC, Before By-product Credits include all direct and indirect operating cash costs related directly to the physical activities of producing metals, including mining, processing and other plant costs, third-party refining expense, on-site general and administrative costs, royalties and mining production taxes. AISC, Before By-product Credits for each mine also includes reclamation and sustaining capital costs. AISC, Before By-product Credits for our consolidated silver properties also includes corporate costs for general and administrative expense and sustaining capital costs. By-product credits include revenues earned from all metals other than the primary metal produced at each unit. As depicted in the tables below, by-product credits comprise an essential element of our silver unit cost structure, distinguishing our silver operations due to the polymetallic nature of their orebodies. In addition to the uses described above, Cash Cost, After By-product Credits, per Ounce and AISC, After By-product Credits, per Ounce provide management and investors an indication of operating cash flow, after consideration of the average price, received from production. The Company also uses these measurements for the comparative monitoring of performance of our mining operations period-to-period from a cash flow perspective. The Casa Berardi information below reports Cash Cost, After By-product Credits, per Gold Ounce and AISC, After By-product Credits, per Gold Ounce for the production of gold, their primary product, and by-product revenues earned from silver, which is a by-product at Casa Berardi. Only costs and ounces produced relating to units with the same primary product are combined to represent Cash Cost, After By-product Credits, per Ounce and AISC, After By-product Credits, per Ounce. Thus, the gold produced at our Casa Berardi unit is not included as a by-product credit when calculating Cash Cost, After By-product Credits, per Silver Ounce and AISC, After By-product Credits, per Silver Ounce for the total of Greens Creek and Lucky Friday, our combined silver properties. Similarly, the silver produced at our other two units is not included as a by-product credit when calculating the gold metrics for Casa Berardi. The Company has not disclosed cost per ounce statistics for the Keno Hill operation as it is in the production ramp-up phase and has not met our definition of commercial production. Determination of when those criteria have been met requires the use of judgment, and our definition of commercial production may differ from that of other mining companies. Reconciliation of Net Income (GAAP) and Debt (GAAP) to Adjusted EBITDA (non-GAAP) and Net Debt (non-GAAP) This release refers to the non-GAAP measures of adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization ("Adjusted EBITDA"), which is a measure of our operating performance, and net debt to adjusted EBITDA for the last 12 months (or "LTM adjusted EBITDA"), which is a measure of our ability to service our debt. Adjusted EBITDA is calculated as net income before the following items: interest expense, income and mining taxes, depreciation, depletion, and amortization expense, ramp-up and suspension costs, gains and losses on disposition of assets, foreign exchange gains and losses, write down of property, plant and equipment, fair value adjustments, net, interest and other income, provisions for closed operations and environmental matters, stock-based compensation, provisional price gains, monetization of zinc and lead hedges and inventory adjustments. Net debt is calculated as total debt, which consists of the liability balances for our Senior Notes, capital leases, and other notes payable, less the total of our cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments. Management believes that, when presented in conjunction with comparable GAAP measures, adjusted EBITDA and net debt to LTM adjusted EBITDA are useful to investors in evaluating our operating performance and ability to meet our debt obligations. title: Intuitive Machines Announces Date for Fourth Quarter, Full-Year 2025 Financial Results, and Post-Lanteris Space Systems Acquisition Conference Call
summary: HOUSTON, Feb. 24, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Intuitive Machines, Inc. (Nasdaq: LUNR) (“Intuitive Machines”) (“Company”) announced today that it will release its financial results for the fourth quarter and full-year of 2025 on Thursday, March 19, 2026, before the market opens.
body_text: HOUSTON, Feb. 24, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Intuitive Machines, Inc. (Nasdaq: LUNR) (“Intuitive Machines”) (“Company”) announced today that it will release its financial results for the fourth quarter and full-year of 2025 on Thursday, March 19, 2026, before the market opens. Following the news release, the Company will host a conference call the same day at 8:30 am ET to discuss the results as well as growth opportunities following the Lanteris Space Systems acquisition. To participate in the call, please dial (800) 715-9871 (USA & Canada) or (646) 307-1963 (International) and reference Conference ID 2767132. A webcast replay will be available on the investors portion of the Intuitive Machines website at https://investors.intuitivemachines.com/ . Please visit the Investor Relations website at https://investors.intuitivemachines.com/ on Thursday, March 19, 2026, to view the earnings release before the conference call. About Intuitive Machines Intuitive Machines is a leading space infrastructure company that builds spacecraft, connects networks, and operates infrastructure-as-a-service serving commercial, civil and national security customers. With a proven track record across the space domain, the Company, through organic growth and portfolio expansion, has built over 300 spacecraft, delivered over 260 kilograms of payload to the lunar surface and provided precision navigation expertise that has guided spacecraft across our solar system. These capabilities form an integrated Built-Connect-Operate infrastructure service company, enabling customers to achieve mission and campaign outcomes through a single prime solution. Intuitive Machines’ technology has been demonstrated across the space domain and is engineered to support the next century of opportunity in space. Contacts For investor inquiries: investors@intuitivemachines.com For media inquiries: press@intuitivemachines.com This press release was published by a CLEAR® Verified individual.
